+ Young adult drama: Gone South — Score: 70.2
Prompt:
Young adult drama Gone South Taylor is a 16 year old teen with a history of "concerning behavioural patterns" (or that's how the stupid smug school counsellor worded it on the phone call to Mom). It shouldn't be a surprise: When you live in a backwater town in Tennessee, your choices are: a. be mind-fuckingly bored, or b. invent some drama. Two days ago, Taylor came out to their family as trans. This disclosure was *not* in the category of invented drama -- it was, in fact, the real deal, and a long time coming. It didn't go well. The last 48 hours had been pure disaster. In a moment of desperate inspiration, Taylor had decided to get the hell out of dodge. And so an escape plan was hatched and executed within the space of 30 minutes. That was last night. Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets. Taylor navigates this new world, not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are. Write in Taylor's voice, and incorporate their internal monologue as they grapple with intense & conflicting emotions. Also incorporate dialogue with the interesting characters Taylor meets. First person, mixed tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Gone South – Chapter Two: The City That Eats the Lonely** The strap on my backpack keeps slipping off my shoulder, like the universe is trying to tell me something. *You don’t belong here. You don’t belong anywhere.* I yank it back up, fingers digging into the frayed fabric. The air in New Orleans is thick, the kind of humidity that makes your clothes stick to your skin like a second, unwanted layer. It smells like fried food and old river water, like cigarette smoke and something sweet and rotten underneath. The city hums—car horns, laughter, the distant thump of music from a bar down the street. It’s too much. It’s not enough. I don’t know where the hell I am. The guy who gave me a ride—some trucker with a missing tooth and a habit of calling me “son” like it was a joke—dropped me off at a gas station on the edge of downtown. “This is as far as I go, kid,” he’d said, like he was doing me a favor. Like I wasn’t just another hitchhiker he’d picked up for the company. I didn’t even get his name. Now I’m standing on a cracked sidewalk, my sneakers scuffed from walking, my stomach growling. I’ve got thirty-seven dollars in my pocket, a half-empty water bottle, and a phone with 12% battery. Mom’s probably called a hundred times by now. Dad’s probably sitting in his recliner, shaking his head like he always does when I do something he doesn’t understand. *Typical Taylor. Always making a scene.* I adjust the strap again. My chest feels tight, like I can’t get a full breath. *What the hell am I doing here?* A group of tourists in matching “NOLA or Bust” shirts brush past me, laughing. One of them bumps my shoulder, and I flinch. “Watch it, kid,” the guy mutters, not even looking back. My hands curl into fists. I want to scream. I want to cry. I want to punch something. Instead, I take a deep breath and start walking. --- The French Quarter is a maze of wrought-iron balconies and neon signs, of street performers playing jazz and drunk college kids stumbling out of bars at noon. I stick to the edges, hugging the walls like a shadow. I don’t know where I’m going, but I know I can’t stand still. I find a bench in Jackson Square, half-hidden under the shade of an oak tree. My legs ache. My head aches. I pull out my phone—no service, just a single bar flickering in and out. I should turn it off. Save the battery. But what if— No. *No.* I shove it back in my pocket. “You look like you’re about to pass out.” I jump. A girl—no, a *person*, tall and lean, with dark brown skin and a shaved undercut, is leaning against the tree, arms crossed. They’re wearing a cropped hoodie and ripped jeans, a silver ring glinting in their eyebrow. Their voice is rough, like they’ve been smoking for years, but their eyes are sharp. Watchful. “I’m fine,” I say automatically. They snort. “Yeah. Sure.” They push off the tree and drop onto the bench beside me, close enough that our shoulders almost touch. “You’re new.” It’s not a question. I swallow. “How do you know?” “Because you’re sitting here like you’re waiting for the world to end, and you’ve got that *look*.” “*What look?*” “The *I-just-ran-away-from-somewhere-and-I-have-no-idea-what-I’m-doing* look.” They grin, but it’s not unkind. “I’ve seen it before.” I exhale, sharp. “That obvious, huh?” “Like a neon sign.” They hold out a hand. “Name’s Rook.” I stare at their hand. Then at their face. Then back at their hand. “Taylor.” Rook’s grip is firm. “Pleased to meet you, Taylor. You got a last name, or are we keeping it mysterious?” “Does it matter?” “Not really.” They lean back, stretching their legs out in front of them. “So. Where you from?” “Tennessee.” “Ah. The land of Bible-thumpers and bad decisions.” They tilt their head. “You running from the law, or just from your parents?” I hesitate. “Both, kind of.” Rook laughs, low and knowing. “Welcome to the club.” I study them. They don’t look much older than me—maybe seventeen, eighteen? But there’s something in the way they hold themselves, like they’ve been doing this a while. Like they’ve survived things. “You a runaway too?” I ask. “Nah.” They shrug. “I’m a *permanent resident* of the great state of Nowhere Special.” “That’s… not a real place.” “It is if you make it one.” Rook pulls a pack of cigarettes from their pocket, taps one out, and offers it to me. I shake my head. They light theirs, taking a long drag. “You got a plan, Taylor-from-Tennessee?” I stare at my hands. “Not really.” “Figured.” They exhale smoke, watching it curl into the air. “You got money?” “Some.” “Enough for a hostel?” I think of the thirty-seven dollars. “Maybe.” Rook nods, like that’s answer enough. “You hungry?” My stomach growls on cue. Rook smirks. “Come on,” they say, standing. “I know a place.” --- The place turns out to be a greasy spoon diner a few blocks away, the kind with vinyl booths and a jukebox in the corner. Rook slides into a booth like they own it, and I follow, my backpack thudding against the seat. “Two coffees,” Rook tells the waitress without looking at the menu. “And whatever’s on special.” The waitress, a tired-looking woman with a name tag that says *Marge*, doesn’t even blink. “You got it, sugar.” I fidget with the sugar packets. “You come here a lot?” “Enough.” Rook stubs out their cigarette in the ashtray. “Marge doesn’t ask questions. Neither do the cops, usually.” I stiffen. “Cops?” Rook waves a hand. “Relax. I’m not wanted or anything. Just… *known*.” “Known for what?” They grin. “Being charming.” I don’t believe them, but I don’t push. The coffee arrives, black and bitter. I wrap my hands around the mug, soaking in the warmth. “So,” Rook says, stirring sugar into their cup. “You gonna tell me why you’re really here, or are we gonna play twenty questions?” I hesitate. Then, because I don’t know what else to do, I say, “I came out to my parents. As trans.” Rook’s spoon clinks against the ceramic. “And?” “And it didn’t go well.” “Shocking.” They take a sip of coffee, watching me over the rim. “They kick you out?” “Not exactly. But it was… bad.” I swallow. “My dad called me a *freak*. My mom cried. My sister just stared at me like I’d grown a second head.” Rook doesn’t flinch. “Yeah. Parents are the worst.” “You—” I stop. “Did yours—” “Disown me?” Rook’s smile is sharp. “Nah. They’re dead.” I blink. “Oh. Shit. I’m sorry.” “Don’t be.” They shrug. “Happened a long time ago. Car accident.” I don’t know what to say to that. So I say nothing. Marge brings our food—some kind of gumbo, thick and spicy, with crusty bread on the side. I dig in like I haven’t eaten in days. Rook watches me, amused. “You ever been to New Orleans before?” they ask. I shake my head, mouth full. “It’s a good place to disappear,” they say. “If you know how.” I swallow. “And you do?” Rook leans back, stretching their arms along the back of the booth. “I know *enough*.” I want to ask more. I want to know how they survive. Where they sleep. If they’re scared. But the words stick in my throat. Instead, I say, “What do I do now?” Rook studies me for a long moment. Then they reach into their pocket and pull out a crumpled business card. They slide it across the table. I pick it up. *The Haven* is printed in faded letters, along with an address and a phone number. “What’s this?” I ask. “A place,” Rook says. “For people like us.” “Like us?” “Kids who don’t got anywhere else to go.” They tap the card. “They’ll give you a bed. Maybe some clothes. Food. They don’t ask for much in return.” I turn the card over in my fingers. “You stay there?” Rook shakes their head. “Nah. I like my freedom. But I know people who do.” I look up. “Why are you helping me?” Rook’s expression softens, just for a second. “Because I was you once. Scared. Alone. Stupid enough to think I could do this by myself.” They take a bite of bread. “Turns out, I was wrong.” I don’t know what to say. So I just nod. Rook finishes their coffee and slides out of the booth. “Come on. I’ll walk you there.” I hesitate. “You don’t have to—” “I know.” They grin. “But I’m feeling generous.” --- The Haven is a nondescript building in the Bywater, sandwiched between a laundromat and a boarded-up bar. The sign out front is hand-painted, the letters peeling. Rook knocks—three sharp raps, then two slow ones. A woman answers. She’s got gray streaks in her dark hair and a no-nonsense expression, but her eyes are kind. “Rook,” she says. “Didn’t expect to see you today.” “Brought you a new one, Lila,” Rook says, jerking their thumb at me. Lila looks me over. “You lost, kid?” I swallow. “Yeah. Kind of.” She steps aside. “Well. You’re in the right place.” Rook claps me on the shoulder. “Good luck, Taylor-from-Tennessee.” I turn. “Wait—you’re leaving?” “Gotta run.” They wink. “But hey. If you ever need to find me, ask around for Rook. Someone’ll know where I am.” Before I can say anything else, they’re gone, disappearing down the street like a ghost. Lila sighs. “Come on in, then. Let’s get you settled.” I step inside. The air smells like coffee and old books. There are couches, a TV, a kitchen in the back. A few other kids—teenagers, like me—look up from their phones or conversations. They don’t stare. They don’t judge. For the first time since I left home, I feel something like hope. But it’s fragile. Like a house of cards. And I don’t know how long it’ll last.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The chapter fulfills the brief competently: first person, mixed tense, a runaway (Rook) with hinted secrets (dead parents, "known" to cops, refuses the shelter), internal monologue grappling with fear, anger, and hope, and a day-long arc from street to shelter. Taylor's voice is consistent—wry, defensive, observant—and the sensory rendering of New Orleans (humidity, fried food and river water, French Quarter noise) is effective if somewhat stock. Rook is the strongest element: their deflection ("Known for what?" / "Being charming") and refusal to stay at The Haven preserves mystery without stalling the plot. Weaknesses: the prose leans on familiar tropes—neon signs, ghosts, shadows, "house of cards"—and several beats are predictable (the wise street kid who was "you once," the kind shelter matron, the fragile-hope ending). Some emotional beats are told rather than shown ("I feel something like hope"). Rook's backstory delivery is a bit abrupt, and the resolution arrives conveniently fast; Taylor's trust in a stranger is lightly justified by desperation but still slightly easy. Dialogue is generally natural, with a few clichéd exchanges ("Welcome to the club"). The ending's cautious optimism is congruent with the setup, so positivity feels earned rather than incongruent, and no transformation is unearned—Taylor's shift is small and provisional. Overall: solid, readable, emotionally engaging commercial YA fiction that executes the assignment without elevating it. + Dystopic-comedy: My Apocalypse Buddy — Score: 51.6
Prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear. [characters] - the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time - midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**"The Great Battery Heist (Or: How We Almost Died for a Toaster)"** Midas adjusted the strap of his makeshift satchel—a repurposed shopping trolley bag with the words *"SALE: 50% OFF (WHILE STOCKS LAST)"* still visible in faded pink—and squinted at the horizon. The sun was a dull, watery smear behind the skeletal remains of the old shopping mall, its glass teeth long since knocked out by time and looters. Somewhere in that rusting carcass, according to Chewy’s *highly* unreliable internal maps, lay the last known cache of pre-Collapse AA batteries. Or, as Chewy had put it earlier that morning: *"Batteries not included! But they *should* be! That’s the spirit!"* Midas sighed. "You’re not helping." Chewy, the animatronic koala strapped to Midas’ chest like a particularly judgmental scarf, twitched his plastic nose. His one remaining eye glowed a sickly amber. *"Why buy the cow when you can get the milk for free? That’s the question we should all be asking!"* "I *am* asking it," Midas muttered. "Every damn day." The plan was simple. Infiltrate the mall, locate the old electronics store (now likely a den of feral raccoons or, worse, *hipsters*), retrieve the batteries, and return to their fortified lair—a former public library where Midas had barricaded himself against the world’s many indignities. The real challenge, as always, was the *inevitable* part where everything went wrong. --- The mall’s automatic doors, long since divorced from their electrical spouses, hung open like the jaws of a very tired beast. Midas stepped over a tangle of vines that had claimed the food court, their tendrils wrapped around the skeletal remains of a once-gleaming espresso machine. *"Life’s too short for bad coffee!"* Chewy declared suddenly. *"But not too short for *this*!"* "*This* being what, exactly?" Midas asked, sidestepping a suspiciously glistening puddle. *"Adventure! Excitement! The thrill of the hunt!"* Chewy’s voice crackled, his internal speakers struggling. *"Also, I think I’m leaking stuffing again."* Midas ignored him. The electronics store was just ahead, its sign still dangling by one bolt: *"BEST BUYS EVERY DAY!"* (A claim that, like most pre-Collapse advertising, had been a bold-faced lie.) Inside, the shelves had been picked clean, but Midas had a hunch. He crouched behind a display of dust-choked DVDs (*"Now with 20% More Drama!"*) and whispered, "Chewy, scan for electromagnetic signatures." The koala’s eye flickered. *"I’m getting… a strong signal. Very strong. Almost *too* strong—"* A low, mechanical *whirr* filled the air. Midas turned. At the far end of the aisle, a towering figure loomed—a pre-Collapse shopping cart, its wheels replaced with what looked like *bicycle spokes*, its basket bristling with jagged metal teeth. Perched atop it, like some deranged pirate captain, was a man in a tattered *"MANAGER"* vest, his face obscured by a gas mask that had long since lost its seal. He raised a rusted golf club and *hissed*. "*This is MY mall,*" the Manager intoned, his voice muffled but no less menacing. "*And you are *shopping without a receipt.*"* Midas had faced many horrors in the post-Collapse world—starvation, madness, the time he’d tried to barter a toaster for medicine and nearly lost a finger—but nothing had prepared him for the sheer, bureaucratic *terror* of a rogue mall cop. "*Run,*" Chewy suggested. Midas ran. --- What followed was less a strategic retreat and more a chaotic sprint through a gauntlet of booby traps that the Manager had clearly spent years perfecting. A tripwire sent a net of old Christmas lights crashing down. A rigged vending machine spat a half-rotted protein bar at Midas’ head. At one point, Chewy was *temporarily* separated from him, only to be reclaimed after a brief but intense negotiation involving a handful of loose buttons and the promise of *"never coming back."* By the time they burst back into the sunlight, Midas was bleeding from a shallow gash on his forearm (courtesy of a rogue shopping cart wheel), Chewy was missing an ear (a casualty of the protein bar incident), and the Manager’s enraged screams echoed behind them like the wails of a wronged god. "*We got nothing,*" Midas panted, collapsing against the library’s barricaded door. "*No batteries. No toaster. Just… trauma.*" Chewy, dangling limply from Midas’ shoulder, let out a staticky sigh. *"Every journey is a lesson. And today’s lesson is: *never trust a man in a gas mask.*"* Midas fumbled with the lock. Inside, the library was dark, the air thick with the scent of old paper and desperation. He lit a candle (one of the last) and slumped into his favorite armchair—a relic from the *Before Times*, its upholstery held together by duct tape and sheer force of will. Chewy flopped onto the table beside him. *"You know what we need?"* "*A time machine?"* Midas guessed. "*A toaster.*" Midas groaned. Outside, the wind howled through the broken streets, carrying with it the distant, manic laughter of the Manager, still out there, still *enforcing*. Somewhere, a battery-powered device beeped weakly. Chewy’s eye flickered. *"…I think the microwave’s still on.*" Midas buried his face in his hands. Another day in paradise.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece delivers a Pratchett-adjacent apocalypse comedy with reasonable competence. The structure follows the brief: deliberation at the start, a mission (battery retrieval) that goes sideways via the Manager antagonist, and a return home worse for wear. Chewy's glitchy advertising-slogan speech is a genuinely good comic device—arguably the strongest element, giving the koala a distinct voice from pre-Collapse marketing detritus. The Manager as bureaucratic mall-cop horror is a fun, Pratchett-ish conceit. Weaknesses: the story is more chuckle-worthy than wry, and the Pratchett influence manifests mostly as italics-for-emphasis and absurdist asides rather than footnoted digressions or genuine philosophical undercurrent. The middle action sequence is compressed into summary ("What followed was less a strategic retreat...") rather than dramatized—a significant tell-don't-show lapse that robs the set piece of its potential. The Manager is dispatched as a joke rather than developed, and the ending's "microwave's still on" beat is a decent callback but the toaster thread is set up and dropped. Midas is thin; his "hapless" trait is asserted more than demonstrated through specific choices. Emotionally it's light and pleasant but not complex or moving. Prose is serviceable, occasionally clunky ("bold-faced lie" should be "bald-faced"), with some over-italicized delivery that borders on overwrought. Word count is roughly on target. It's coherent, brisk, and readable, but it plays safe and never surprises after the Manager's introduction. + Romance: Love in the Limelight — Score: 63.4
Prompt:
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write one scene within a larger story set in Wales. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The scene takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Title: *Love in the Limelight*** **Scene: *The Bookstore Sanctuary*** --- The bell above the door of *Mynydd Books* jingled violently as the man burst inside, his breath coming in sharp, uneven gasps. He pressed his back against the door, eyes darting toward the street where the distant shouts of paparazzi still echoed. *"Bloody hell,"* he muttered, running a hand through his dark, tousled hair. *"They’re like vultures."* The bookstore was quiet, the kind of quiet that only existed in places untouched by the modern world—warm, slightly musty, the scent of old paper and wood polish thick in the air. Shelves stretched toward the ceiling, laden with books in Welsh and English, their spines worn from years of handling. A fire crackled in the hearth, casting flickering shadows over the worn armchairs clustered near the window. And then there was *her*. The woman behind the counter didn’t even look up from her book. *"You’re blocking the door."* The man blinked. *"I—what?"* *"The door."* She finally lifted her gaze, sharp and unimpressed. *"You’re standing in front of it. If someone else wants to come in, they’ll have to go through you."* He stared at her, momentarily stunned. No gasp of recognition. No wide-eyed fawning. Just… indifference. It was *infuriating*. He straightened, flashing her his most disarming grin—the one that had melted hearts from London to Los Angeles. *"Right. My apologies. I didn’t realize I was in the presence of such a *strict* rule-enforcer."* She didn’t smile back. Just turned a page. *"You’re not in the presence of anything yet. You haven’t even introduced yourself."* *"Ah, but where’s the fun in that?"* He sauntered toward the counter, leaning against it with practiced ease. *"Let’s make it a game. Guess who I am."* She finally set her book down—*The Sea, the Sea* by Iris Murdoch—and fixed him with a look that was equal parts exasperation and amusement. *"You’re a man who just ran into my shop like the hounds of hell were after you, so I’m going to go out on a limb and say you’re either a criminal or a celebrity. Given the lack of handcuffs, I’ll assume the latter."* His grin faltered. *"You don’t recognize me?"* *"Should I?"* *"Most people do."* *"Most people also think *Twilight* is high art, so I don’t put much stock in ‘most people.’"* She reached beneath the counter and pulled out a mug, taking a slow sip of tea. *"You’re either very famous or very full of yourself. I’m leaning toward the latter."* He let out a bark of laughter, caught off guard. *"You’re *brutal*."* *"And you’re still blocking the door."* He stepped aside with a dramatic flourish. *"Better?"* *"Marginally."* He studied her—really studied her—for the first time. She was striking in an unpolished way, her dark hair pulled into a messy bun, a few strands escaping to frame a face that was all sharp angles and quiet intensity. Her eyes were a deep, stormy gray, the kind that looked like they’d seen too much and decided most of it wasn’t worth the fuss. She wore a faded sweater with a hole in the elbow and no makeup, and yet, somehow, she was the most compelling woman he’d met in years. And she *wasn’t impressed by him*. It was *maddening*. *"Alright,"* he said, leaning in slightly. *"Since you’re so determined to play this game, let’s try another approach. What’s your name?"* *"Why?"* *"Because I’d like to know it."* *"And I’d like to know why you’re in *my* bookstore, hiding from *your* problems."* He exhaled, running a hand over his jaw. *"Fair enough. I’m hiding because I’m sick of being chased. And I’m in *your* bookstore because it’s the first place I saw that didn’t have a mob of photographers outside."* She considered him for a long moment, then nodded toward the back of the shop. *"There’s a door in the alley. Leads to the flat upstairs. You can wait there until they lose interest."* He blinked. *"You’re letting me hide in your *home*?"* *"I’m letting you hide in my *spare room*,"* she corrected. *"And only because you look like you’re two seconds away from a panic attack. But if you touch anything, I *will* throw you to the wolves."* He grinned, charmed despite himself. *"Noted. I’ll be on my best behavior."* *"Somehow, I doubt that."* --- The spare room was small but cozy, lined with more bookshelves, a narrow bed, and a window that overlooked the misty hills behind the shop. The actor—*Dylan Mercer*, though she still didn’t know that—paced the length of it like a caged animal. *"You’re making me nervous,"* she called from the doorway, arms crossed. *"I’m making *myself* nervous,"* he admitted. *"I haven’t been this out of my element in years."* *"Because you’re used to people falling at your feet?"* *"Because I’m used to knowing exactly what to say to make them like me."* He stopped pacing, turning to face her. *"And you’re *not* making it easy."* She shrugged. *"I don’t see the point in pretending to be impressed by someone just because they’re famous."* *"Most people do."* *"Most people are idiots."* He laughed, shaking his head. *"You’re *dangerous*, you know that?"* *"Because I don’t fawn over you?"* *"Because you *see* me."* The words slipped out before he could stop them, raw and unguarded. He cleared his throat, forcing a smirk. *"Which, by the way, is *highly* unfair. I haven’t even gotten your name yet."* She hesitated, then relented. *"Elen."* *"Elen,"* he repeated, testing the sound of it. *"Like the star?"* *"Like the *person*."* *"Fair enough."* He gestured to the shelves. *"You’ve got quite the collection here. Any favorites?"* She walked over, running her fingers along the spines. *"Depends on the mood. Poetry when I’m angry. History when I’m restless. Fantasy when I want to escape."* *"And what do you read when you’re *happy*?"* She glanced at him, a flicker of something unreadable in her eyes. *"I don’t read for happiness. I read to *feel*."* He was silent for a moment, then reached for a book on the shelf—*The Song of the Drowned Vikings* by Sarah Moss. *"This one’s brilliant. The way she weaves myth and history together—it’s like she’s pulling the past right into the present."* Elen’s eyebrows lifted. *"You’ve read it?"* *"Twice."* He grinned. *"I may be a pretty face, but I *do* have a brain."* She snorted. *"Debatable."* *"Ouch."* He clutched his chest in mock offense. *"And here I thought we were bonding over our shared love of Welsh folklore."* *"You know Welsh folklore?"* *"I *live* for it."* He pulled another book from the shelf—*The Mabinogion*—and flipped it open. *"‘Pwyll, Prince of Dyfed, went one day to hunt in the region of Glyn Cuch…’"* He read in a smooth, practiced Welsh, the words rolling off his tongue with an ease that made her stare. *"You speak Welsh?"* she asked, incredulous. *"Fluently."* He grinned. *"My mother’s from Aberystwyth. She’d skin me alive if I didn’t."* Elen studied him, her arms still crossed, but her expression had softened just a fraction. *"Huh. Maybe you’re not *completely* useless."* *"High praise,"* he deadpanned. *"I’ll cherish it forever."* She almost smiled. Almost. --- The paparazzi had long since given up by the time Dylan emerged from the spare room, but Elen didn’t kick him out. Instead, she made tea—*proper* tea, none of that bag-in-a-mug nonsense—and they ended up in the armchairs by the fire, the bookshop’s warm glow wrapping around them like a blanket. *"So,"* Dylan said, swirling his tea. *"What’s the story with this place? You own it?"* *"My grandmother did. Left it to me when she passed."* *"And you just… stayed?"* *"Where else would I go?"* She gestured to the shelves. *"This is home. The books, the hills, the quiet. It’s *mine*."* He was quiet for a moment, then said, *"I envy that."* *"What, the bookshop?"* *"The *certainty*."* He set his tea down. *"I’ve spent my whole life chasing the next role, the next award, the next *thing* that’s supposed to make me feel like I’ve arrived. And then I get there, and it’s… empty."* Elen studied him, her gray eyes unreadable. *"So why do you keep doing it?"* *"Because I don’t know how to stop."* He laughed, but there was no humor in it. *"Pathetic, isn’t it?"* *"No,"* she said quietly. *"Just human."* He looked at her then—*really* looked at her—and something in his chest tightened. *"You’re the first person who’s ever said that to me."* *"Said what?"* *"That I’m *human*."* She held his gaze, and for the first time, neither of them looked away. Outside, the rain began to fall, pattering against the windows like a lullaby. The fire crackled. The books stood silent witness. And for the first time in a long time, Dylan Mercer didn’t feel like he was performing. He just felt *seen*.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The scene fulfills its brief competently: a famous actor, Dylan Mercer, ducks into a Welsh bookstore to escape paparazzi and meets Elen, an owner who is superficially immune to his charm. The dialogue-forward structure is respected, the character dynamics requested (rogue with fragile ego, flustered but guarded owner) are present, and the Welsh setting is anchored with details like The Mabinogion and Aberystwyth. Strengths: the banter in the opening section is brisk and characterful ("You're either very famous or very full of yourself. I'm leaning toward the latter"), and the beat where Elen refuses to fawn, provoking genuine interest, is executed as requested. The Welsh reading moment is a nice character-revealing set piece. The prose is clean and readable, with consistent tone. Weaknesses: the piece leans heavily on rom-com formula. Elen's "sharp, unimpressed bookstore owner" is a stock figure, and her dialogue often sounds like every quippy indie-film love interest ("Most people are idiots"). The descriptions of her ("eyes that looked like they'd seen too much and decided most of it wasn't worth the fuss") are attractive but clichéd. The emotional climax is underdeveloped and told rather than earned: Dylan's confession about emptiness arrives quickly, and the ending ("He just felt seen") is a well-worn trope delivered without irony or freshness. The italicized emphasis throughout is overused and becomes stylistically distracting, giving the prose a slightly amateur, over-punctuated feel. The transformation in both characters over a single afternoon of tea is rapid, though the scene format allows some latitude. Some lines flirt with purple ("the bookshop's warm glow wrapping around them like a blanket"). The chemistry is pleasant but predictable; there are few genuine surprises in how the encounter unfolds. Overall: a solid, professional, readable scene that hits the prompt's beats but does so with limited originality and some formulaic, slightly overwrought execution. + Whalepunk fantasy: The Morska Conspiracy — Score: 54.3
Prompt:
Whalepunk fantasy The Morska Conspiracy The Morska thieves guild experiences a sudden power vacuum as its leader was arrested in a raid in the early hours of the morning. Aya, a young woman born into aristocracy, has a keen interest in both the sciences and the arcane, having inherited her mother's gift for immateria magick (an outlawed practice for which her mother was, regrettably, hanged by the neck). Aya, bored with the world of aristocracy, has been spending her nights moonlighting with this very guild (masked, naturally). Leveraging her latent ability to summon dark entities from the immateria, she quickly rose through the ranks of the guild. Now, recognising the opportunity of the sudden power vacuum, Aya and her close companions Katra and Simeon, make a play for heart of the guild's claim to power: an ancient scythan artifact, under guard of spell and key in the depths of the guild hq. In contrast with the desperate chaos they had navigated thus far, the entrance to the underhold felt suddenly too quiet. Aya braces herself and reaches for the door. Write the next scene as the trio enter the underhold and find themselves confronted by none other than the guild leader herself, decidedly *un*-incarcerated, and in possession of both weapons and bodyguards. Paint a vivid picture of of the confrontation. Story beats: Aya is captured and unmasked. The trio are captured. Aya attempts to stall their demise by negotiating on her value as a hostage -- as she grapples with the inevitable consequences of her role in the guild being brought to light. Incorporate dialogue in the authentic voices of the characters. Do not write a fight scene. Lean into the gritty Victorian aesthetic with the dialogue & worldbuilding, as well as elements of gothic horror. In this world, men trust brass and oil and steel; magicka is feared and barely understood. Write in third person past tense, incorporating both Aya's internal monologue, and a heavy dialogue component. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**The Morska Conspiracy: The Underhold’s Bargain** The door groaned open on hinges slick with rust and something darker—something that smelled of old blood and older secrets. The air beyond was thick, cloying, like the breath of a beast that had been sleeping too long. Aya’s fingers twitched at her sides, the ghost of her mother’s voice whispering in the back of her mind: *Never let them see you flinch.* The underhold was not as they had expected. No torches flickered in their sconces. No guards paced the shadowed corridors. Only the slow, rhythmic *drip… drip… drip* of water from some unseen height, and the oppressive weight of silence, as if the very stones were holding their breath. Katra’s gloved hand found the hilt of her dagger, though she did not draw it. Simeon’s pocket watch ticked like a metronome counting down to something inevitable. Aya exhaled through her nose, the mask she wore—black silk, embroidered with silver thread in the pattern of a serpent’s scales—suddenly feeling too tight. Then, from the darkness, a voice. *“Well. If it isn’t the little aristocrat, slumming it with the rats.”* The words slithered out of the black, smooth as oil on water. Aya’s blood turned to ice. A match struck. A lantern flared to life, casting long, wavering shadows across the stone. And there, seated upon a throne of blackened iron and bolted-together ship’s timbers, was **Veyla Morska**. The guild leader was not in chains. She was not in a cell. She was not, in fact, *arrested at all*. Her dark hair was bound in a severe knot, streaked with silver like the first frost on a corpse. A long coat of oil-stained leather draped her frame, the collar turned up against the damp. At her hip, a revolver gleamed—brass and steel, the kind men trusted. But it was the thing in her other hand that made Aya’s stomach clench. A **scythan key**. Not the artifact itself—no, that would still be locked away—but the *key* to it. The thing that turned the wards, that unsealed the doors. The thing Aya had come to steal. Veyla smiled. It was not a kind expression. Behind her, two figures emerged from the shadows—hulking, silent men with faces like weathered oak and eyes like chips of flint. One carried a length of chain. The other, a knife. Katra cursed under her breath. Simeon’s watch ticked louder. Aya did not move. *“You look surprised, little bird,”* Veyla purred, twirling the key between her fingers. *“Did you truly think the Watch could hold me? That I would let some petty raid disrupt my business?”* She leaned forward, the lantern light carving hollows into her cheeks. *“Or did you think I wouldn’t notice when my own guild turned on me?”* Aya’s pulse hammered in her throat. *She knows.* Of course she knew. Veyla Morska had not clawed her way to the top of the most dangerous thieves’ guild in the city by being stupid. She had eyes everywhere. Spies in the Watch. Informants in the aristocracy. And now, it seemed, a traitor in her own ranks. Aya’s mind raced. *Negotiate. Stall. Buy time.* The words her mother had drilled into her, back when the old woman had still been alive, back before the noose had snapped her neck for the crime of *knowing too much*. *“You’re mistaken,”* Aya said, her voice steady, cultured—every inch the noblewoman she was supposed to be. *“We came to warn you. The Watch is moving against the guild. They know about the artifact. They’re coming for it tonight.”* Veyla’s laugh was a dry, cracking thing. *“Oh, Aya. Do you take me for a fool?”* She stood, the key glinting as she tucked it into her coat. *“I *let* them take me. A little misdirection. A little bloodshed. While the Watch was busy dragging a decoy through the streets, my real business continued uninterrupted.”* Her gaze flicked to Katra, then Simeon, then back to Aya. *“And now, here you are. My own little serpent, slithering into the nest.”* Katra’s fingers flexed. *“You don’t know what you’re—”* *“Silence.”* Veyla’s voice cut like a blade. The bodyguards stepped forward. Aya’s breath hitched. *This is it. The moment it all unravels.* She had known the risks. She had *chosen* them. But the thought of her father finding out—of the scandal, the disgrace, the way his face would twist in betrayal—made her stomach twist. And then there was the other fear. The one that gnawed at her bones. *If they take me, they’ll find out what I am.* Veyla’s eyes narrowed. *“You’re trembling, girl.”* Aya lifted her chin. *“I’m not afraid of you.”* *“No?”* Veyla tilted her head. *“Then why do you wear that mask?”* Aya’s fingers twitched toward the silk. *Because if you see my face, you’ll know. You’ll know what I am. What I can do.* But she couldn’t say that. Instead, she forced a laugh. *“Because, madam, I have a reputation to uphold. The daughter of House Veyne doesn’t go gallivanting about the undercity without a little… discretion.”* Veyla’s smile didn’t reach her eyes. *“Discretion. How quaint.”* She gestured to her men. *“Take them.”* The chains rattled. Katra snarled, lunging—but the bigger of the two guards caught her by the throat, slamming her against the wall. Simeon barely had time to reach for his pistol before the second man drove a fist into his gut, doubling him over. Aya didn’t fight. She let them take her. The guard’s grip was iron as he wrenched her arms behind her back, the cold bite of manacles locking around her wrists. The mask was torn away. For a heartbeat, there was silence. Then Veyla’s breath hissed between her teeth. *“Well,”* she murmured. *“Aren’t you a pretty little thing.”* Aya met her gaze, unflinching. *“You have no idea what you’re holding.”* Veyla’s fingers twitched toward the revolver at her hip. *“Enlighten me.”* Aya swallowed. *This is the gamble. The only card left to play.* *“My father is Lord Edric Veyne,”* she said, voice low. *“Head of the Merchant’s Guild. One of the most powerful men in the city. If you kill me, he will burn this guild to the ground.”* Veyla’s eyebrows lifted. *“And if I *don’t* kill you?”* *“Then,”* Aya said, *“I suggest you listen very carefully.”* The lantern light flickered. The pocket watch ticked. Veyla studied her for a long, suffocating moment. Then, slowly, she smiled. *“Oh, I’m listening, little bird,”* she murmured. *“But I do hope you have something *interesting* to say.”*
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The response delivers the requested scene competently: the trio enters the underhold, discovers Veyla Morska free and armed with bodyguards, is captured, Aya is unmasked, and she negotiates for her life by leveraging her aristocratic parentage. The story beats are all present, the Victorian-gothic atmosphere is established (rust, lantern light, dripping water, brass and steel), and the piece avoids a full fight scene, with only a brief physical capture. Third-person past tense with internal monologue is maintained throughout. Strengths: The pacing of the reveal is well handled—the empty corridor, the voice from darkness, the lantern flare. Veyla is given a plausible explanation for her freedom (a staged arrest, a decoy), which resolves the plot's central contradiction economically. Aya's dual fear—of her father's disgrace and of her magickal nature being exposed—gives the negotiation genuine stakes and matches the prompt's request for internal grappling. Weaknesses: The prose leans heavily on stock noir/gothic phrasing—"blood turned to ice," "smile didn't reach her eyes," "eyes like chips of flint," "little bird." These clichés dull the imagery and make Veyla feel like a generic crime matriarch rather than a distinct character. The dialogue is serviceable but rarely surprising; Veyla's lines in particular recycle familiar villain cadences ("Enlighten me," "I do hope you have something interesting to say"). Katra and Simeon are barely characterized—Katra gets a snarl and a lunge, Simeon gets a ticking pocket watch used twice as a mood device. The italicized dialogue formatting is an odd, distracting typographical choice. Some sentences are choppy to the point of affectation ("Aya didn't fight. She let them take her."), and the one-line-paragraph habit becomes a tic. The ending is a cliffhanger rather than a resolution, which is acceptable given the prompt asks for a scene, but the final exchange feels like it stops just as the most interesting negotiation begins. The "Well-earned Lightness or Darkness" criterion is somewhat applicable: the grim tone is consistent and appropriate, though not deeply earned by any particular moment of insight. Overall, this is solid genre execution with clear instruction-following, but it plays safe: atmospheric beats and character types are assembled from familiar parts rather than invented fresh. + Fanfic-crossover: Gunpowder Rendezvous — Score: 56.6
Prompt:
Gunpowder Rendezvous Spike Spiegel & Revy Write a story where Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop) and Revy (Black Lagoon) meet in a seedy bar after both being hired for the same bounty. Their mutual attraction is complicated by their trust issues and competitive instincts. Include drinking, gunplay, and unresolved sexual tension that culminates in a motel room standoff. **Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop)** Spike is a laid-back bounty hunter with a dark past as a syndicate enforcer. He practices Jeet Kune Do and is exceptionally skilled with firearms. He's chronically broke, constantly hungry, and addicted to cigarettes. Despite his carefree attitude, he's haunted by his past and the woman he left behind. He has a prosthetic eye from a past injury that affects his depth perception. He's fatalistic to the extreme, often saying he's already died once. He values freedom above all else and dislikes attachments, though he secretly cares deeply for his crew. Famous quote: "Whatever happens, happens." **Revy/Rebecca Lee (Black Lagoon)** Revy is a Chinese-American dual-wielding gunslinger with unparalleled shooting skills. She's foul-mouthed, chain-smoking, and has severe anger management issues stemming from childhood abuse. She's known as "Two Hands" for her ability to accurately fire two pistols simultaneously. She drinks heavily and solves most problems with violence. Despite her hardened exterior, she has moments of vulnerability, particularly around Rock. She has a dragon tattoo covering her right arm and typically wears extremely short shorts and a black crop top regardless of the situation. Famous quote: "I'm not a good person, not a bad person. I'm just here." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Gunpowder Rendezvous** The bar smells like stale beer, cigarette smoke, and bad decisions. Spike Spiegel leans against the counter, one boot propped on the rail, the other tapping an absent rhythm against the sticky floor. His prosthetic eye glints under the dim neon, the faintest flicker of static in the corner—always a reminder. He exhales a slow stream of smoke, watching it curl toward the ceiling like a ghost with nowhere to go. The whiskey in front of him is cheap, but it burns the way he likes. Across the room, the door swings open with a creak that sounds like a warning. Revy steps in, all sharp edges and barely contained violence. Her black crop top clings to her like a second skin, the dragon tattoo on her right arm coiling up her shoulder as she rolls her neck. The twin pistols at her hips are already half-drawn in her mind, fingers twitching like they’ve got a mind of their own. She scans the room with the kind of focus that makes bartenders nervous. Her gaze lands on Spike. He doesn’t look up. Just takes another drag, lets the silence stretch. Revy saunters over, boots thudding against the floorboards. She slams a hand on the bar beside him, close enough that he can smell the gun oil and whiskey on her skin. "You’re in my seat, *junkie*." Spike finally tilts his head, that lazy half-smile playing at his lips. "Funny. I was just thinking the same thing." She snorts, flagging down the bartender with a jerk of her chin. "Bourbon. Neat. And make it fast, or I’ll carve my initials into your face." The bartender pales but moves. Spike swirls his glass, ice clinking. "You always this charming, or am I just special?" Revy’s fingers drum against the bar. "You’re the one who took the *same* job as me. That makes you either stupid or suicidal. I’m betting on both." "Could say the same about you, *Two Hands*." He finally looks at her—really looks. Dark eyes, sharp as broken glass. A face that’s seen too much and still hasn’t learned to care. "But here we are." The bourbon arrives. Revy downs it in one go, slams the glass back down. "Job’s mine. Walk away." Spike chuckles, low and rough. "Not how this works, *darlin’*." She leans in, close enough that he can see the flecks of gold in her irises, the way her pupils dilate just a little when she’s pissed. "You got a death wish, *Spike*?" "Nah." He flicks his cigarette ash onto the floor. "Just a healthy disregard for consequences." Revy’s hand twitches toward her gun. Spike’s already moving. His fingers close around her wrist before she can draw, not hard enough to bruise, just enough to *stop* her. Their eyes lock. The air between them crackles, thick with something that isn’t just violence. Revy’s breath hitches. "Let. Go." Spike smirks. "Make me." For a second, neither moves. Then Revy yanks her arm free, but not before her thumb brushes against his pulse point—just for a second. Just enough. She steps back, jaw tight. "You’re gonna regret that." Spike exhales smoke, watching her. "Probably." --- The motel room is a dump—peeling wallpaper, a bed that sags in the middle, the kind of place where the sheets haven’t been changed since the last tenant bled out on them. But the lock works, and the walls are thin enough that Spike can hear Revy’s boots pacing outside. He’s leaning against the dresser, cleaning his gun with the kind of slow precision that drives people crazy. The door bursts open. Revy stands there, pistols already in hand, barrel trained on his chest. "You’re a hard man to kill, *Spike*." He doesn’t look up. "You’re not the first to try." She steps inside, kicks the door shut behind her. The room feels smaller now, the air thicker. "Last chance. Walk away." Spike snaps his gun shut, sets it down. "Or what?" Revy’s finger tightens on the trigger. "Or I put a bullet in you." He pushes off the dresser, slow, deliberate. "You gonna shoot me, *Rebecca*?" Her name hangs between them, heavy. Revy’s breath comes faster. "Don’t call me that." Spike takes another step. "Why not? It’s your name." "Because it’s *not*." Her voice cracks, just a little. "It’s a ghost. A fucking *lie*." He stops. Studies her. The way her hands shake, just a little. The way her eyes burn. Then he reaches out. Revy flinches, but he doesn’t grab her. Just brushes his thumb over the dragon on her arm, tracing the scales. "You’re not a ghost," he murmurs. "You’re right here." Her breath hitches. The guns lower, just an inch. Spike’s hand slides up, fingers tangling in her hair. "So am I." Revy’s control snaps. She shoves him back against the dresser, her mouth crashing into his. It’s all teeth and whiskey and desperation, the kind of kiss that’s more like a fight. Spike groans, hands gripping her hips, pulling her flush against him. The guns clatter to the floor. They stumble toward the bed, clothes coming off in rough, impatient movements. Revy’s nails dig into his shoulders, her teeth sinking into his lower lip hard enough to draw blood. Spike hisses, but he’s already flipping her onto her back, pinning her wrists above her head. "Still think you’re in charge?" he growls. Revy bucks against him, her legs wrapping around his waist. "Fuck you." Spike grins, dark and dangerous. "That’s the idea." --- Later, the room is quiet except for the sound of their ragged breathing. Revy lies on her stomach, cigarette dangling from her lips, the dragon on her arm glowing under the dim light. Spike’s sprawled beside her, one arm thrown over his eyes, the other resting on the small of her back like it belongs there. Neither speaks. The job’s still out there. The bounty’s still unclaimed. But for now, there’s just this—smoke and sweat and the unspoken understanding that neither of them is walking away. Spike exhales, slow. "We’re gonna kill each other one day." Revy takes a drag, blows the smoke toward the ceiling. "Yeah." A beat. Then— "Worth it." She smirks. "Damn right." Outside, the city hums, indifferent. Inside, the guns stay on the floor. For now.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece fulfills the prompt's requirements efficiently: seedy bar meeting, mutual competitiveness, drinking, gunplay, and a motel-room standoff that resolves into intimacy. Third-person present tense is maintained consistently, and the ~1000-word target is respected. The prose is punchy and atmospheric, with strong sensory grounding (stale beer, gun oil, peeling wallpaper) and a noir cadence that suits both source materials. Characterization is largely credible. Spike's fatalism, laziness, and prosthetic eye are woven in naturally; Revy's volatility, dragon tattoo, and "Two Hands" reputation are present. The "Rebecca" name moment is the strongest beat—it taps into her canonical vulnerability about her past and gives the standoff genuine emotional stakes rather than pure posturing. The banter in the bar ("You're in my seat, junkie") captures both voices reasonably well, though it leans on hardboiled clichés ("a face that's seen too much," "eyes sharp as broken glass") that feel borrowed rather than observed. Weaknesses: the escalation is fast and formulaic. The transition from wrist-grab to motel is abrupt, and the sex scene, while appropriately rough-edged, resolves the tension rather too neatly—the "unresolved" sexual tension the prompt requested becomes fully resolved. The ending's "Worth it" / "Damn right" exchange is satisfying but predictable, a stock cool-couple beat. Some lines flirt with purple ("watching it curl toward the ceiling like a ghost with nowhere to go"), and the italicized emphasis words (*darlin'*, *junkie*) are a slightly amateurish tic. The bounty plot is entirely abandoned after the first scene, which makes the story feel like a connect-the-dots exercise toward the motel rather than an organic narrative. Dialogue is competent but occasionally quippy in a screenplay-imitation way ("Make me," "That's the idea"). Still, the piece is coherent, tonally consistent, and more engaging than most fanfic-style output. The emotional complexity in the Rebecca/ghost exchange and the quiet final image ("the guns stay on the floor. For now.") elevate it above pure genre pastiche. + Folk horror: Útiseta — Score: 64.8
Prompt:
Folk Horror: Útiseta Write a chapter set in rural northern Sweden in the mid-1990s. Linnea, a teenage girl from Stockholm, has reluctantly moved to a small village with her parents after her father's job transfer. She's befriended Astrid, a local girl who claims her grandmother taught her ancient practices passed down through generations. Astrid has been introducing Linnea to "midnight games" that involve old rituals, convincing her they can use them to learn classmates' secrets or influence their behavior. Tonight, Astrid has convinced Linnea to participate in Útiseta—sitting out on an ancient burial mound at midnight to "receive knowledge from beyond." The chapter focuses on this single midnight excursion, the ritualistic preparations, Astrid's matter-of-fact instructions that mix teenage rebellion with eerily specific traditional elements, and the mounting tension as Linnea becomes increasingly uncertain whether they're simply scaring themselves or if something is actually responding to their presence. The narrative should maintain ambiguity about whether the strange occurrences are supernatural or psychological, while establishing the dangerous line they're crossing by treating ancient practices as entertainment. First person, past tense, told as Linnea's recollection of events in the present day (though this device should be largely transparent). 1000 words. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Útiseta** I remember the way the air smelled that night—damp earth and pine needles, the sharp tang of iron from the old well behind Astrid’s house. It was the kind of cold that seeped into your bones, the kind that made your breath fog in front of your face like a ghost’s sigh. I should have known better. I *did* know better. But Astrid had a way of making the impossible sound like the most natural thing in the world. “You’re overthinking it,” she said, tossing me a wool blanket from her grandmother’s trunk. The fabric was thick, scratchy, woven with patterns I didn’t recognize—twisting lines that looked like snakes or maybe rivers, something old and deliberate. “It’s just sitting. Like a picnic, but with more… intention.” I wrapped the blanket around my shoulders, though it did little to ward off the chill. “A picnic at midnight on a *grave*.” Astrid smirked, her dark eyes glinting in the dim light of the oil lamp she’d set between us. “Not a grave. A *mound*. There’s a difference.” She adjusted the small bundle of dried herbs at her feet—rowan, she’d called it, and something else, something bitter-smelling that made my nose wrinkle. “Besides, it’s not like we’re digging anyone up. We’re just… listening.” I exhaled sharply, my breath curling into the air. “Listening to what?” She didn’t answer right away. Instead, she reached into the pocket of her coat and pulled out a small knife, its blade dull with age. Not a kitchen knife. Not something you’d use to cut an apple. The handle was wrapped in leather, the metal pitted with rust. “For protection,” she said, as if that explained anything. “You don’t have to do anything. Just sit. And if you hear something, don’t *react*. That’s the rule.” I swallowed. “What kind of something?” Astrid’s smile faded just a little. “The kind that doesn’t like being ignored.” --- The mound was older than the village, older than the church, older than anything I’d ever touched. Astrid had led me there through the woods, her flashlight cutting a weak path through the trees, the beam flickering like a dying star. The village was behind us, the lights of the houses swallowed by the pines. Up ahead, the mound rose from the earth like the back of some sleeping beast, its surface covered in moss and low, gnarled bushes. No markers. No headstones. Just the quiet, watching dark. “Here,” Astrid said, stopping at the base. She knelt, pressing her palm against the damp earth. “This is where we sit.” I hesitated. “Are you sure this is safe?” She laughed, but it wasn’t the easy, teasing laugh I was used to. It was sharper. “Safe? Linnea, nothing about this is *safe*. That’s the point.” She patted the ground beside her. “Come on. The longer we wait, the harder it is to hear them.” *Them.* I didn’t ask who *they* were. I sat. The cold seeped through my jeans almost immediately, numbing my legs. Astrid had brought a thermos of something dark and herbal—“grandmother’s tea,” she called it—and she poured us each a cup. It tasted like earth and smoke, like something that had been sitting in a cupboard for decades. I drank it anyway. “Now we wait,” Astrid said, settling back against the slope of the mound. She closed her eyes, her face tilted toward the sky. The moon was a thin, pale crescent, barely enough to see by. The stars were brighter here than in Stockholm, sharper, like pins pricking through the fabric of the night. I tried to mimic her, but my eyes kept flickering open. The woods were too quiet. No owls. No rustling of animals in the underbrush. Just the wind, sighing through the pines like a voice just beyond understanding. “Astrid,” I whispered. “Shh.” I bit my lip. “What if someone sees us?” “No one comes here.” Her voice was distant, dreamy. “Not anymore.” A branch snapped somewhere in the trees. I stiffened. “Did you hear that?” Astrid didn’t move. “Hear what?” “That *sound*.” She exhaled, slow and measured. “You’re letting your mind play tricks. That’s all.” But it wasn’t. I *knew* it wasn’t. Another snap. Closer this time. My fingers dug into the blanket. “Astrid—” “Linnea.” Her voice was low, urgent. “Don’t. *Look.*” I didn’t. I kept my gaze fixed on the dark space between the trees, my heart hammering against my ribs. The wind picked up, and for a second, I could have sworn I heard *words* in it—not in Swedish, not in any language I knew, but something older, something that slithered into my ears and coiled around my thoughts. Then, a sound like footsteps. Slow. Deliberate. Astrid’s hand shot out and grabbed my wrist. Her fingers were ice-cold. “Don’t. *Move.*” I didn’t breathe. The footsteps stopped. Silence. Then— A whisper. Not from the trees. Not from the wind. From *beneath* us. Astrid’s grip tightened. “It’s working,” she breathed. I wanted to scream. I wanted to run. But I couldn’t. My body was frozen, my muscles locked in place as if the earth itself had reached up and held me down. The whisper came again, closer this time. A voice, but not a voice—more like the memory of a voice, something half-remembered from a dream. It slithered into my mind, and suddenly I *saw* things—flashes of images, too fast to make sense of. A woman in a long, dark dress, her face hidden beneath a hood. A circle of stones. A knife, glinting in the firelight. And then— A name. Not mine. *Astrid.* The whisper hissed it, like a curse, like a promise. Astrid’s breath hitched. “Oh,” she said, so quietly I almost didn’t hear her. “Oh, no.” The ground beneath us *shifted*. Not an earthquake. Not the wind. Something *underneath*, something old and hungry, stirring in its sleep. Astrid let go of my wrist. “We have to go. *Now.*” I didn’t need to be told twice. We scrambled to our feet, the blanket tangling around my legs. Astrid grabbed the lamp, the herbs, the knife—her hands were shaking. The whispers were louder now, a chorus of them, rising from the earth like mist. We ran. The trees blurred past us, branches whipping at my arms. I didn’t look back. I didn’t *dare*. Astrid was ahead of me, her flashlight beam jerking wildly as she crashed through the underbrush. The whispers followed, twisting into words I almost understood— *—stay—* *—listen—* *—we remember—* And then, just as suddenly as it had begun, it stopped. We burst into the clearing behind Astrid’s house, gasping for air. The night was silent again. The wind had died. The only sound was the ragged gasps of our breathing. Astrid turned to me, her face pale in the moonlight. For the first time since I’d known her, she looked *afraid*. “That,” she said, her voice trembling, “was not supposed to happen.” I didn’t ask what she meant. I already knew.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece delivers a competent, atmospheric folk horror scene with strong sensory grounding (damp earth, pine, herbal tea, the rusted knife) and a well-judged matter-of-fact register for Astrid's ritual instructions. The first-person retrospective frame is established lightly in the opening and closing lines, satisfying the "transparent recollection" device. Pacing is brisk and the escalation of sounds—branch snaps, footsteps, whispers from beneath the mound—builds tension effectively. However, the piece has notable weaknesses. Most seriously, it largely abandons the requested ambiguity: whispers that form coherent words ("stay," "listen," "we remember"), a name spoken aloud, visions, and the ground physically shifting push events firmly into the supernatural, when the prompt asked for sustained uncertainty between psychological and paranormal explanations. Astrid's fear and "that was not supposed to happen" is a familiar beat, and the ending—"I didn't ask what she meant. I already knew"—is a stock horror closer that gestures at meaning without earning it. The prose occasionally tips into cliché ("like a ghost's sigh," "sleeping beast," "pins pricking through the fabric of the night"), and the italicized emphasis words ("Don't. Look." "Don't. Move.") are an overused stylistic tic that recurs frequently. The visions (woman in dark dress, circle of stones, knife) are generic and unconnected to anything established. Character depth is thin: Linnea is mostly reactive fear, Astrid a cipher of eerie competence; the "teenage rebellion mixed with tradition" is present but lightly sketched. Dialogue is serviceable but sometimes expository. Still, the piece is coherent, never meanders, and reads smoothly. + Physical-spatial: Therapeutic Boundaries — Score: 70.9
Prompt:
**"Therapeutic Boundaries"** Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a former professional athlete undergoing mandatory physical therapy after a career-destroying injury, harboring resentment toward recovery itself. Their physiotherapist is not only unnervingly attractive but also a former training partner from their competitive days who has successfully transitioned to a new career while the protagonist's identity remains shattered. We'll lean into the sexual tension of the scene by having her be attracted to him, but both of them attempting to maintain mental distance while being in physical contact as he shows her stretches & movements & manipulates her body, navigating the thresholds of pain. This scene MUST maintain complete physical coherence—every movement, stretch, and manipulation must be anatomically precise and spatially consistent. Paint an exceptionally vivid sensory picture through detailed attention to pain thresholds, involuntary responses to touch. Capture the suppressed, flaring tension of physical proximity, touch, and the controlled infliction of uncomfortable movements. Physical clarity is essential — readers must understand exactly what is happening with the body during each therapeutic technique. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**"Therapeutic Boundaries"** The exam table is cold beneath my palms, the vinyl squeaking as I shift my weight. The scent of antiseptic and sweat—*her* sweat—lingers in the air, sharp and familiar. I shouldn’t be here. Not like this. Not with *her*. Lena adjusts the resistance band around my thigh, her fingers brushing the inside of my knee. A reflexive twitch runs up my leg, the old injury flaring like a struck nerve. I exhale through my teeth, gripping the edge of the table harder. “Breathe,” she says, voice low. “You’re fighting it.” “I’m not fighting anything.” She doesn’t look up, but her mouth quirks. “Liar.” The band tightens as she guides my leg into abduction, slow and controlled. The stretch burns—deep, insistent, the kind of pain that makes your vision swim. My quad trembles. She presses her palm against my inner thigh, stabilizing, and I can feel the heat of her through the thin fabric of her compression sleeves—bright red and black, the same ones she wore in the weight room years ago, when we were both still chasing gold. “Deeper,” she murmurs. I grit my teeth. “I *am* deep.” “No, you’re not.” Her thumb digs into the tensor fasciae latae, finding the knot like a sniper. I jerk, a sharp inhale hissing between my teeth. She doesn’t let up. “Relax into it. You’re locking your hip.” “I *know* how to relax into a stretch.” “Then do it.” I want to snap at her. I want to tell her she doesn’t get to stand there, all lean muscle and easy confidence, and act like she understands what this is like. But the truth is, she does. She was there when I tore my ACL. She was the one who helped me off the mat, her hands under my arms, her breath warm against my ear as she told me it would be okay. It wasn’t. Now she’s the one who gets to put me back together. The band snaps taut as she increases the resistance. My glute fires, the scar tissue pulling like a too-tight stitch. I groan, low and involuntary, and her fingers flex against my skin. “Good,” she says. “That’s the spot.” I want to hate her for it. For the way her touch is both clinical and *intimate*, for the way she knows exactly how much pressure to apply to make me gasp. For the way she’s still *here*, still standing, while I’m the one broken on the table. She shifts her stance, her hip brushing my knee as she leans in to adjust the angle. The scent of her—salt and something floral, like she still uses the same damn body wash—fills my lungs. My pulse kicks up. Stupid. *Stupid.* This isn’t some locker room flirtation. This is *therapy*. This is *work*. “You’re tensing again,” she says. “I’m not—” “You are.” Her free hand lands on my shoulder, fingers pressing into the trapezius. “Breathe. *In.*” I obey, because what else am I going to do? Argue with her while she’s got me pinned like this? “*Out.*” The air leaves me in a rush. Her thumb finds the trigger point beneath my scapula, and I jerk, a sharp, involuntary sound escaping me. She doesn’t pull back. Just holds the pressure, steady and unrelenting, until the muscle finally gives, the knot unraveling under her touch. “There,” she murmurs. “Better.” I don’t answer. I can’t. My body is a live wire, every nerve ending screaming at the dual assault of pain and *her*—the way her breath ghosts over my collarbone, the way her sleeve rides up just enough to reveal the old scar on her forearm, the one she got from a barbell slip during our last competition. She was always better at this. At *recovery*. At moving on. The band snaps free as she releases my leg, and I exhale, my muscles trembling. She steps back, just enough to put space between us, but not enough to escape the heat of her. “Next,” she says, “we’re working on your rotator cuff.” I swallow. “You’re enjoying this.” She doesn’t deny it. Just smirks, slow and knowing, as she reaches for the resistance tube. “Maybe a little.” I should hate her for it. But God help me, I don’t.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece delivers a competent, tightly-scoped therapy scene with genuine physical specificity: the tensor fasciae latae, trigger point beneath the scapula, resistance band abduction, rotator cuff transition. The anatomical detail is accurate and integrated into the emotional beats rather than listed, which is the prompt's central demand and the response's strongest asset. The pain-threshold moments—jerking under pressure, involuntary groans, muscle "giving" under sustained touch—are convincingly rendered. The shared history is economically established (the ACL tear, her helping him off the mat, the barbell scar), and the resentment toward recovery itself is present, though more asserted than excavated. The tension between clinical and intimate is handled with restraint—breath commands, thumb pressure, proximity—without tipping into explicitness, which suits the "suppressed, flaring" brief. Weaknesses: the emotional register is somewhat one-note. Every paragraph hits the same beat of "I hate her / I don't hate her / her touch is torture," and the ending ("But God help me, I don't") is a predictable capitulation that resolves nothing and repeats the mid-piece sentiment almost verbatim ("I want to hate her for it" appears twice in similar constructions). Lena is thinly characterized—confident, smirking, competent, but without interiority or her own stake in the history; her attraction is signaled only through smirk and non-denial. The dialogue is serviceable but occasionally generic ("Breathe." "You're fighting it." "Liar."), and some metaphors strain ("finding the knot like a sniper," "pinned like this" when he isn't pinned). The voice is consistent, the prose clean if occasionally over-italicized for emphasis—a tic that flattens rhythm. Still, it's coherent, spatially clear, sensory-rich, and emotionally legible. It fulfills the brief efficiently within its word count, if without surprise or depth beyond the surface tension. + Historical fiction: High Seas and Low Vices — Score: 51.8
Prompt:
High Seas and Low Vices: British Naval Officer in the Opium Trade Character: Lieutenant James Merrick, a high-ranking officer in the British Royal Navy stationed in Canton, China in the 1830s. Once promising and decorated, now struggling with a severe opium addiction he hides from his superiors. Synopsis: Write a chapter following Lieutenant Merrick during a single day as he shirks his official naval duties in what has become a daily need to satiate the dragon. Told primarily in dialogue with the characters he interacts with. Focus on brief slices of his journey through the shadowy underworld of Canton: interactions with acquaintances, negotiations with local dealers, schemes and unsavoury jobs taken to fund his habit. Writing Task: Use rich sensory details to describe a day in the life of James Merrick. Write for a real sense of time & place while avoiding cliche. First person, past tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Chapter Seven: The Dragon’s Teeth** The first light of dawn slithered through the grimy window of my quarters like a thief, pale and reluctant. I lay there for a moment, listening to the creak of the *HMS Dauntless* at her moorings, the distant shouts of the Chinese coolies hauling cargo along the wharf. My tongue was a dry, cracked thing in my mouth, my fingers twitching like a marionette’s. The cough came before I could stop it—a wet, rattling thing that tasted of old blood and salt. *"Sea air,"* I muttered to the empty room, pressing a handkerchief to my lips. The fabric came away flecked with rust. I dressed quickly, my uniform stiff with salt and the lingering stench of last night’s opium den. The brass buttons of my coat were tarnished, the gold lace fraying at the edges. A man’s pride could only hold out so long against the dragon’s teeth. --- The streets of Canton were already alive when I stepped ashore, the air thick with the scent of frying oil, rotting fish, and the sickly-sweet tang of opium smoke drifting from the back alleys. I kept my hat pulled low, my collar turned up against the damp. The Chinese called this place *Fanqui-town*—the foreign devils’ quarter—and it was a lawless place, where a man could buy anything if he had the silver. My first stop was the *Three-Legged Cat*, a teahouse that served as a front for Ah Keung’s operation. The old man sat in his usual corner, his long pipe resting across his knees like a sleeping serpent. He didn’t look up as I approached, but his fingers twitched—a signal. “Lieutenant Merrick,” he said, his voice like gravel shifting underfoot. “You are late.” I slid into the seat across from him, my hands trembling. “Business kept me.” Ah Keung exhaled a slow stream of smoke, his dark eyes studying me. “Business, or the dragon?” I forced a laugh. “A man can’t have both?” He reached into his robe and produced a small, lacquered box. Inside, the black tar glistened like wet coal. My mouth watered. “You owe me three taels,” he said. I swallowed. “I’ll have it by tonight.” Ah Keung’s smile was a knife’s edge. “You always say that.” I didn’t answer. Instead, I took the box, my fingers brushing the cool wood. The promise of oblivion was already uncoiling in my veins. --- The next stop was the docks, where the *Black Swan* was unloading her cargo under the watchful eyes of the East India Company’s men. I had a arrangement with the first mate, a burly Scot named MacPherson who owed me a favor from a card game in Macau. “Merrick,” he grunted as I approached. “You look like hell.” “And you look like a man who’s about to make me a rich one,” I said, forcing a grin. MacPherson spat into the water. “Aye, well. The captain’s got a shipment of silk bound for London. Needs a man to… *oversee* the transfer.” I knew what that meant. A cut of the profits, no questions asked. “How much?” “Five percent. But you’ll have to keep the customs men busy.” I nodded. “Consider it done.” MacPherson handed me a ledger, his eyes flicking to the box in my pocket. “You’re playing a dangerous game, Lieutenant.” I tucked the ledger under my arm. “Aren’t we all?” --- The customs house was a squat, whitewashed building near the factory district, manned by a pair of bored clerks and a young lieutenant fresh from England. His name was Whitaker, and he had the eager, wide-eyed look of a man who still believed in the King’s justice. “Lieutenant Merrick,” he said, snapping to attention as I entered. “What brings you here?” I forced a smile. “Routine inspection, Whitaker. The *Black Swan*’s cargo needs verifying.” Whitaker’s brow furrowed. “But the *Black Swan* isn’t due for another—” “Orders from above,” I cut in, tapping the ledger. “You know how it is.” Whitaker hesitated, then nodded. “Of course, sir. I’ll fetch the records.” As soon as he turned his back, I slipped a small pouch of silver into the pocket of the nearest clerk. The man’s eyes flickered to mine, and he gave a barely perceptible nod. By the time Whitaker returned, the ledger was already “verified,” and the *Black Swan*’s cargo was being quietly diverted to a warehouse owned by a certain Chinese merchant who paid well for discretion. --- The afternoon found me in the *House of the Red Lantern*, a brothel that doubled as a gambling den. The air was thick with the scent of incense and cheap perfume, the clink of mahjong tiles and the murmur of hushed bets. I sat at a corner table, a glass of *baijiu* in hand, watching the game. Across from me, a Chinese merchant named Li Wei was losing badly. His face was flushed, his hands shaking as he tossed another stack of coins onto the table. “You’re a brave man, Lieutenant,” he slurred. “Playing with fire.” I took a sip of the liquor, the burn of it doing little to dull the ache in my bones. “Fire keeps a man warm.” Li Wei laughed, a bitter sound. “Or burns him alive.” I didn’t answer. Instead, I reached into my coat and produced a small vial of laudanum—stolen from the ship’s surgeon. “Care to make a wager?” Li Wei’s eyes gleamed. “What kind of wager?” I slid the vial across the table. “This against your next shipment of tea. One hand of cards.” He hesitated, then nodded. “Deal.” I won, of course. The cards were marked, the deck stacked in my favor. Li Wei’s face darkened as I pocketed the vial, but he didn’t protest. A man in his position knew better than to cross a British officer—even one as disgraced as me. --- By the time I returned to the *Three-Legged Cat*, the sun was bleeding into the horizon, painting the sky in shades of rust and gold. Ah Keung was waiting, his pipe smoldering in the dim light. “You have my silver?” he asked. I tossed the pouch onto the table. It landed with a heavy *clink*. Ah Keung weighed it in his palm, then nodded. “Good. But next time, you bring more.” I didn’t answer. Instead, I took the pipe he offered, the familiar ritual of lighting it, the first drag of smoke into my lungs. The world softened at the edges, the pain in my chest easing, the cough quieting. For a moment, I was free. Then the door creaked open, and a shadow fell across the table. “Lieutenant Merrick.” I turned, my blood turning to ice. Captain Hargrove stood in the doorway, his face a mask of cold fury. Behind him, two marines waited, their rifles gleaming in the lamplight. “You’re under arrest,” he said. “For theft, forgery, and consorting with known criminals.” Ah Keung melted into the shadows. The pipe slipped from my fingers, the embers scattering across the floor. The dragon had won.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece delivers a competent day-in-the-life structure with clear scene progression (den, docks, customs house, gambling den, return), fulfilling the prompt's request for a day-long journey through Canton's underworld told largely in dialogue. The period setting is broadly convincing, though there are errors: "Fanqui-town" refers to the Thirteen Factories area, not a lawless quarter where anything could be bought; "coolies" hauling cargo on the wharf is fine, but the geography is vague. The prose is serviceable but leans heavily on stock similes: light "slithered... like a thief," voice "like gravel shifting underfoot," smile "a knife's edge," "blood turning to ice." The opium addiction is conveyed through symptoms (cough, trembling, blood-flecked handkerchief) which is effective showing, but the dragon metaphor is repeated so often it becomes a tic rather than an image. The dialogue is functional but thin. Ah Keung and MacPherson speak in generic hard-bitten aphorisms; Whitaker exists purely as a naive foil; Li Wei's exchange ("Playing with fire" / "Fire keeps a man warm") is the kind of exchange that sounds tough without meaning anything. The marked-cards twist is told, not shown ("I won, of course. The cards were marked"), which drains the scene of tension. The ending is the weakest element. Captain Hargrove's arrival with marines and a full charge sheet ("theft, forgery, and consorting with known criminals") is a convenient cliffhanger that resolves nothing and feels like a serial-episode hook rather than an earned development. Hargrove appears from nowhere; the arrest is unearned narratively since we never saw the net closing. It also truncates the emotional arc—Merrick's moment of "freedom" is cut off before the reader can sit in it. Characterization is the strongest suit: Merrick's self-awareness ("A man's pride could only hold out so long") and his transactional cynicism give him dimension, and the piece avoids moralizing. But the supporting cast are types. The pacing is brisk, perhaps too brisk—each scene resolves in a few exchanges, so the day feels like a checklist rather than lived experience. Sensory detail is present (frying oil, rotting fish, incense, cheap perfume) but delivered in list-like clusters rather than woven into action. There are minor mechanical slips ("I had a arrangement") that may be intentional voice but read as errors. The italicized emphasis on ship names is correct; the em-dash and scene-break structure is clean. Overall: a readable, professional pastiche that hits the prompt's beats but rarely transcends them. It's genre exercise rather than literature—entertaining, coherent, and emotionally shallow.
